vocab.articleQuote: Fisk’s flamboyance and Gould’s bribes made the Erie’s watered stock seem obviously crooked.
vocab.inContext: Jim Fisk's loud, showy, attention-grabbing style made the shady stock scheme look as crooked as it was.
vocab.meaning: A confident, colorful, attention-grabbing quality in how someone dresses, behaves, or performs.
examples: The point guard played with such flamboyance that the crowd cheered even his warm-up dribbles.
Her flamboyance showed in the bright, mismatched outfits she wore to every school event.

vocab.articleQuote: It broke faith with the literal, tangible conception of shares.
vocab.inContext: People used to believe a share's value had to match real, touchable property the company owned, like rails and railcars.
vocab.meaning: Able to be touched or physically measured; real and concrete rather than abstract.
examples: After weeks of practice, the team finally saw tangible progress in their times.
She wanted tangible proof she'd finished the chores, so she photographed the clean kitchen.

vocab.articleQuote: The great movement toward corporate concentration might have collapsed and antitrust law would have become almost moot.
vocab.inContext: If holding companies had been outlawed, the whole problem antitrust law was built to fight might have vanished — leaving the law with nothing left to do.
vocab.meaning: No longer relevant or worth arguing about, usually because the situation has changed or the question has already been settled.
examples: Once the game was rained out, the argument over who should start at pitcher became moot.
She'd already accepted the other school's offer, so debating the essay topic was moot.

concepts.name: The Gilded Age
concepts.articleQuote: Appeared in the June 13, 2026, print edition as 'The Invention of the Trillionaire: Gilded Age Blazed a New Path'.
concepts.inContext: The essay's whole cast — Vanderbilt, Drew, Gould, Fisk, Morgan, Rockefeller — and its railroad-and-stock battles all unfold in this era, which the article treats as familiar background.
concepts.meaning: A nickname for the United States from roughly the 1870s to 1900, a time of explosive industrial growth, huge railroad and oil fortunes, and very little regulation. Writer Mark Twain coined the term: 'gilded' means coated in a thin layer of gold, hinting that the dazzling wealth on the surface hid corruption and deep inequality underneath. It's the period that produced America's first giant corporations and its first billion-dollar fortune.

concepts.name: What a share represents
concepts.articleQuote: They broke the link between the value of a share and physical things.
concepts.inContext: Gilded Age financiers shifted the meaning of a stock share away from 'a slice of the company's physical property' toward 'a claim on the company's future earnings.'
concepts.meaning: A share of stock is a unit of ownership in a company. The deep question this essay tells is what that ownership is worth: just the company's tangible stuff (buildings, machines), or its expected future profits, brand, and ideas? Modern markets settled on the second view — which is why a software company that owns little more than laptops can be worth billions.

concepts.name: Watered stock and overcapitalization
concepts.articleQuote: Stock issued beyond construction costs was called “watered stock.”
concepts.inContext: Erie Railway insiders printed far more shares than the railroad's real assets justified, diluting what each share stood for.
concepts.meaning: Issuing shares worth more than a company's actual assets or earnings can support. The name comes from making cattle drink water to weigh more before sale. Today we'd call it inflating a company's value — investors worry the 'extra' shares represent nothing real, so the price can collapse when reality catches up.

concepts.name: Holding company
concepts.articleQuote: ...a holding company—a corporation that exists simply to own other corporations.
concepts.inContext: Jay Gould used a paper company that built nothing to control and combine several railways, sidestepping laws against merging.
concepts.meaning: A company whose main purpose is to own controlling stakes in other companies rather than make products itself. It lets one group quietly control many businesses at once — a structure that powered the huge merger boom of 1897-1904 and is still how many modern corporate empires are organized.

concepts.name: Antitrust law
concepts.articleQuote: The Sherman Antitrust Act may have been designed to rein in corporate power, but it did nothing to slow Rockefeller’s massive accumulation of wealth.
concepts.inContext: The 1890 law was meant to break up monopolies, and in 1911 it forced Standard Oil to split into 33 companies — yet Rockefeller, keeping shares in all of them, only got richer.
concepts.meaning: Laws that try to keep any single company from dominating a market and crushing competition. They're one of the two main tools (the other being the progressive income tax) that Americans built to limit corporate power and concentrated wealth — but as the Standard Oil breakup shows, they don't automatically reduce a founder's fortune.

quiz.question: According to the essay, what 'revolutionary' change made unprecedented Gilded Age fortunes possible?
options: The invention of the railroad
Breaking the link between a share's value and physical things
The Sherman Antitrust Act
The progressive income tax
quiz.explanation: The piece argues fortunes exploded once a share's value was no longer tied only to a company's tangible property.

quiz.question: Where did the term 'watered stock' come from?
options: Railroads running alongside rivers
Diluting wine with water at celebrations
Making cattle drink heavily to weigh more before sale
Watering down ink to print more share certificates
quiz.explanation: The term came from livestock markets, where cattle were made to drink water to weigh more — like issuing shares beyond a company's real worth.

quiz.question: What is a 'holding company,' as the article describes it?
options: A bank that holds customers' deposits
A company that exists mainly to own other companies
A business that only stores goods in warehouses
A company waiting to go public on the stock market
quiz.explanation: Gould used a paper holding company to control multiple railways without formally merging them.

quiz.question: What happened to Rockefeller's wealth after the 1911 antitrust ruling broke up Standard Oil?
options: He lost most of his fortune
His wealth stayed exactly the same
He kept shares in all 33 spun-off companies and grew richer
He was forced to sell all his shares to the public
quiz.explanation: Because he held stock in every spin-off, the combined value soared and he reached his first billion in 1916.

quiz.question: If a question has become 'moot,' what does that mean?
options: It is the most important question of all
It is no longer relevant or worth arguing about
It can only be decided by a court
It is too confusing for anyone to answer
quiz.explanation: Moot means a point is no longer worth debating — the essay says antitrust law could have become almost moot if holding companies had been banned.
